blocks.content: Say you are building the Swiggy app. Behind the scenes there is an orders service, a users service, a payments service, a catalog service, a delivery tracking service, maybe a dozen more.

Now imagine your mobile app calling each of those services directly. It needs to know every service address, retry logic for each one separately, and its own copy of the login check for every single call.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302543-664278072.png
blocks.alt: Client calling three services directly versus through a gateway

blocks.content: That gets messy fast. Add a fourth service next month and every client app on every phone needs an update just to know it exists.
An API gateway puts one front door in front of all your services, so clients only ever talk to one address.
API gateway is the single entry point clients hit instead of talking to microservices directly.
1. Introduction
When you move from one monolith to a bunch of microservices, you solve some problems and create a new one: now there are many places a client has to know about instead of one.

["Problem it solves
Without a gateway, clients hardcode addresses for every service and reimplement auth, retries, and logging for each one.","With a gateway
Clients call one endpoint. The gateway figures out which service should handle it and takes care of the shared plumbing."]
items:
Problem it solves
Without a gateway, clients hardcode addresses for every service and reimplement auth, retries, and logging for each one.

With a gateway
Clients call one endpoint. The gateway figures out which service should handle it and takes care of the shared plumbing.

blocks.title: Why this matters in interviews
blocks.content: Almost every microservices system design question expects you to draw a gateway in front of the services. Leaving it out is one of the most common gaps interviewers flag.
2. What an API gateway does
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302543-726779740.png
blocks.alt: Client hitting one gateway that fans out to three services

blocks.content: At its core, a gateway is a reverse proxy that sits between clients and your services. But it does more than just forward bytes.
2.1 Single entry point

Every client, whether it is a mobile app, a web app, or a third party integration, talks to one host name. The gateway is the only thing exposed to the outside world; the services behind it can live on a private network.
2.2 Request routing
The gateway looks at the incoming request and decides which backend service should actually handle it, then forwards the request there and relays the response back.
2.3 Cross cutting concerns handled once
Authentication, rate limiting, and logging get implemented one time at the gateway instead of copy pasted into every service.
2.4 Response aggregation
Sometimes the gateway calls more than one backend service for a single client request and stitches the results together before replying, so the client makes one round trip instead of several.
3. Request routing at the gateway
Routing is the most basic job of a gateway: given an incoming request, figure out which service owns it.
3.1 Path based routing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302544-148338820.png
blocks.alt: Gateway routing requests by URL path to three services

blocks.content: The gateway looks at the path prefix. A request to slash orders goes to the orders service, slash users goes to the users service, and so on. This is the most common style because one domain can serve every route.
3.2 Host based routing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302544-428344601.png
blocks.alt: Gateway routing requests by subdomain to two services

blocks.content: Some setups route by subdomain instead, so orders dot yoursite dot com and users dot yoursite dot com hit the same gateway but get sent to different backends. This is less common for internal APIs but shows up when different teams own different subdomains.
3.3 A sample route config
Here is roughly what path based routing looks like in a real gateway config, using a Kong style declarative setup.

services:
  - name: orders-service
    url: http://orders-svc.internal:8080
    routes:
      - name: orders-route
        paths: ["/api/orders"]

  - name: pricing-service
    url: http://pricing-svc.internal:8080
    routes:
      - name: pricing-route
        paths: ["/api/pricing"]

  - name: catalog-service
    url: http://catalog-svc.internal:8080
    routes:
      - name: catalog-route
        paths: ["/api/catalog"]

blocks.title: Keep routing rules boring
blocks.content: Routing should be a lookup table, not a decision tree with business rules baked in. If you find yourself writing if statements about order status inside the routing layer, that logic belongs in a service, not the gateway.
4. Cross cutting concerns centralized at the gateway
blocks.text: 4. Cross cutting concerns centralized at the gateway

blocks.content: This is the part that actually saves you the most engineering time. Instead of every service reinventing the same plumbing, the gateway does it once.
4.1 Authentication
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302545-422803538.png
blocks.alt: Every service independently checking auth for a client

blocks.content: Without a gateway, every service has to validate the incoming token itself. That means every team maintains its own copy of the auth logic, and a bug in one copy is a security hole.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302545-844805700.png
blocks.alt: Gateway validating the token once before forwarding

blocks.content: With a gateway, the token gets validated once at the front door. If it is invalid, the request never even reaches a backend service. Valid requests can be forwarded with a trusted internal header so services do not need to re verify the signature.
4.2 Rate limiting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396302546-113807042.png
blocks.alt: Gateway throttling one client while allowing another through

blocks.content: The gateway can track how many requests each client or API key has made and reject requests once they cross a limit, protecting every backend service behind it at once.
4.3 TLS termination
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304071-204703443.png
blocks.alt: Gateway terminating HTTPS and talking plain HTTP internally

blocks.content: The gateway handles the HTTPS handshake and decryption, then talks to internal services over plain HTTP on the private network. Services skip the certificate management overhead entirely.
4.4 Request and response logging

Since every request already passes through the gateway, it is the natural place to log request paths, latencies, and status codes for every call in one consistent format, instead of stitching together logs from a dozen different services.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Auth logic lives in one place, easier to audit","Gateway becomes a dependency every request relies on"],["Rate limits are consistent across all services","Services still need their own logging for internal debugging"],["TLS certs managed in one spot, not per service","A bug in gateway logic can affect every service at once"]]}
5. The bottleneck and single point of failure risk
blocks.text: 5. The bottleneck and single point of failure risk

blocks.content: Putting everything behind one door is convenient, but that door can now break everything if it goes down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304073-336962401.png
blocks.alt: A single gateway instance crashing and taking down all traffic

blocks.content: If your gateway runs as a single instance and it crashes, none of your services are reachable anymore, even if every one of them is healthy. The gateway has become the weakest link in the whole system.
5.1 Scaling and high availability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304073-118388830.png
blocks.alt: Load balancer spreading traffic across two gateway instances

blocks.content: The fix is to treat the gateway like any other critical service: run multiple instances behind a load balancer, keep it stateless so any instance can handle any request, and autoscale it under load.

blocks.title: Do not skip this
blocks.content: Teams sometimes design a beautiful microservices architecture and then run the gateway as a single Nginx box on one server. That one box is now more important than any individual microservice, so it deserves at least the same redundancy.
6. The god object risk
The opposite failure mode is a gateway that does too much. Once you have a central place that touches every request, it is tempting to keep adding logic to it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304073-91503665.png
blocks.alt: A gateway stuffed with pricing rules and order validation logic

blocks.content: Teams start putting pricing calculations, order validation, or feature flag logic directly in the gateway because it is convenient and touches every relevant request anyway. Over time the gateway turns into a second monolith that every team is afraid to touch.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304074-594767996.png
blocks.alt: A thin gateway that only routes, with logic staying in services

blocks.content: The gateway should stay thin. Its job is routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, and logging, the cross cutting stuff. Business logic like pricing rules or order validation belongs in the service that owns that domain.

["Good gateway job: check the token is valid","Good gateway job: route slash orders to the orders service","Bad gateway job: calculate a discount based on order history","Bad gateway job: decide whether an order can be cancelled"]
items: Good gateway job: check the token is valid
Good gateway job: route slash orders to the orders service
Bad gateway job: calculate a discount based on order history
Bad gateway job: decide whether an order can be cancelled

blocks.content: 7. Real systems
You will not usually build a gateway from scratch. A handful of mature products cover almost every use case.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304074-682670969.png
blocks.alt: Four common gateway products all doing routing, auth, and rate limiting

blocks.content: {"headers":["Product","Notes"],"rows":[["Kong","Open source, plugin based, built on Nginx, popular for self hosted setups"],["AWS API Gateway","Fully managed, integrates directly with Lambda and other AWS services"],["Nginx","Can be configured as a lightweight gateway using reverse proxy and upstream blocks"],["Netflix Zuul","Java based gateway from Netflix microservices stack, an early popular choice"]]}

blocks.title: You do not need to memorize every feature
blocks.content: In an interview, naming one or two of these and knowing roughly what a gateway does for you is usually enough. The important part is knowing when to draw one on the whiteboard, not reciting a feature list.
8. Worked example: mobile client, catalog, and pricing
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: mobile client, catalog, and pricing

blocks.content: Say the mobile app needs to show a product page: the product details plus its current price. Without a gateway, the app would call the catalog service and the pricing service separately and merge the results itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396304075-373674083.png
blocks.alt: Gateway calling catalog and pricing then merging the response

blocks.content: With a gateway, the mobile app makes one call to slash api slash product slash id. The gateway calls the catalog service for product details and the pricing service for the current price, waits for both, merges them into one JSON body, and sends that back.

blocks.title: Aggregation handler
blocks.text: A single mobile request triggers two internal calls behind the gateway, but the client only ever sees one request and one response.

blocks.content: Notice the two calls happen in parallel, not one after another. If they ran sequentially, the client would wait for the combined latency of both services instead of just the slower of the two.

blocks.title: Handle partial failure
blocks.content: What happens if pricing is down but catalog works fine? Decide upfront whether to fail the whole request or return catalog data with a placeholder price. Silently returning broken data is the worst option.
9. The interview angle

In a system design interview, once you have drawn more than two or three services, an interviewer expects a gateway to show up in your diagram. It is treated as a default building block, not an advanced trick.

["Mention it early when you sketch multiple services talking to a client","Call out what it centralizes: auth, rate limiting, routing, TLS","Mention that it needs to be highly available itself, not a single box","Keep business logic out of it when asked to go deeper on any one service"]
items: Mention it early when you sketch multiple services talking to a client
Call out what it centralizes: auth, rate limiting, routing, TLS
Mention that it needs to be highly available itself, not a single box
Keep business logic out of it when asked to go deeper on any one service

blocks.content: If your design has five microservices and no gateway, the first question you will get is where clients are supposed to send their requests.
10. Summary

["An API gateway is the single entry point clients use instead of calling microservices directly","It routes requests by path or host to the right backend service","It centralizes auth, rate limiting, TLS termination, and logging","It can aggregate multiple backend calls into one response for the client","It must be scaled and made highly available, or it becomes a single point of failure","It should stay thin and avoid absorbing business logic that belongs in a service","Kong, AWS API Gateway, Nginx, and Zuul are common real world choices"]
items: An API gateway is the single entry point clients use instead of calling microservices directly
It routes requests by path or host to the right backend service
It centralizes auth, rate limiting, TLS termination, and logging
It can aggregate multiple backend calls into one response for the client
It must be scaled and made highly available, or it becomes a single point of failure
It should stay thin and avoid absorbing business logic that belongs in a service
Kong, AWS API Gateway, Nginx, and Zuul are common real world choices

blocks.content: Once you have more than a couple of services, a gateway stops being optional. The question is not whether to have one, it is how thin you can keep it while it does its job well.
